pre_update_snapshot_occurrences.value: This movement originated in the Western Qin Great Revolution of 1810. People of this age viewed it as a modern economic transformation arising within agrarian eastern societies rooted in clan structures. Its method was to confiscate or redeem over-concentrated land from old owners and redistribute it among peasants, thereby freeing resources to the market. In politics, the reforms aim to grab power from old military nobles by physically reduce their wealth and means to control their 'clansmen'. As Northern Ming nobilities, with their highly militarised tradition in local ruling, are widely regarded as the source of chaos and poverty among the people of the old northern regimes. The Chinese imperial ruling bloc once suspended this transformation during its rise. But around Mu Zhongtang's 1820 southern campaign, to revive the economy, liberate production, and mobilize peasants and soldiers from the bottom, Mu and his confidants reopened the movement.

In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

In spring 1678, Zheng Zhao - Duke of Wu in Northern Ming, Nanjing regent and minister of rites - after a chain of military victories at home and abroad, petitioned the court to enter the capital and pay homage to the Ming Son of Heaven. At that time, the Tianjin Prince of Yan, victor of the great constitutional war thirty years earlier, still blazed in power. Yet Zheng's stubbornness overcame counsel and threats alike, and the journey took place that June.

This audience became a grand procession unseen for nearly three centuries, from warlord age to feudal-prince age in Northern Ming. Though coerced by Yan, Qin, and Qi powers into bringing only 5,000 guards and officials, Zheng's train contained elite land-sea forces of Wu's era: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese shield-swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadier units, even an exiled noble group of 'Far Eastern Yin people' seeking troops from the Chinese emperor. It carried treasures won by Wu over a century of global campaigns, plus Annamese and Khmer tribute rice borne by nearly ten thousand laborers. In stark contrast stood the famine-struck Central Plains under transport extortion and local armed strife.

After returning, Zheng Zhao at once took the title 'Supreme One.' Wu then entered rapid growth as refugees from north and south poured into its core and colonies. Zheng and his successors pushed harsh centralizing 'autocratic reform' and land commodification, ultimately securing our foundation as Southern Court overlord directing all nations. Wu's march has never ceased - to this very day...

Chen Dongyang (courtesy name Manyue, 1772-[Date.GetString|v]) was a leading civic republican thinker and founding hero of the short-lived Western Qin revolutionary republic. Exiled from his own state, he worked with southern progressives and became chief architect of Southern Ming modernization as chief minister.

Yet reform brought fierce political upheaval and resistance from local power holders. As reform reached completion, Zheng Qin and allies came to fear republican ideals beyond their control. On [Date.GetString|v], while Chen departed for lecture tours in the Far East Continent, an unidentified Wa ronin shot him dead on deck with a short firearm.

After Chen's death, southern republicans who followed him immediately fell into accusation and factional dispute. Deng Mingyu, minister of revenue and fellow 'Four Gentlemen of the Republic,' moved toward Zheng Qin and the Southern Office. Zheng Diaojin, former administrator of Huguang, led part of the faction west to Sichuan under Xiao Huli.

The Southern Ming turmoil that began with Wu-Ming dynastic transfer reached an unprecedented peak on [Date.GetString|v].

Former Ming loyalists, landlords sacrificed in land reform, and remnants of the early-century civic revolution - three groups with very different aims - united under pressure from the Zheng house of Southern Office. Emperor Tianyan sent Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang, Lin Zexu, and Wu (Ii) Naosuke to suppress them.

When Tianyan took the throne, Southern Ming was nominally the world's leading empire. This upheaval shocked the world at once; from Far East Continent to distant England, states sent envoys. Today those envoys will witness a fierce eastern conflagration rekindled less than half a century after peace.

Rather than full explosion of contradictions, decisive Southern Court politicians delayed imperial collapse through firm choices. Even amid Wu-Ming dynastic upheaval, regional governors chose no effective resistance and accepted Wu narratives of total corruption by the Ming emperor and his magnates, preserving a fragile peace in South China.

In one sense, this implies the sun-and-moon dynasty had long become rotten wood no one wished to die with. Zhu Kuobin, the last emperor to defend court order, may simply have been born at the wrong time.

Yet this survivor of four centuries of warlord politics lost much. The age of war-peace confrontation ended, but opponents, regional prejudice among old feudatory populations, and new radical groups still move in the shadows of the new era, cloaking the nation's road forward in dense fog.

西元1678年春，时为北明吴国公的大明南京留守使、南京礼部尚书的（吴武宗）郑昭在他在海内外的一系列军事胜利后，单方面向朝廷上书，准备进京觐见大明天子。当是时，在三十年前的大宪战争中大获全胜的天津燕主及其国势还如烈火烹油。堪称北明战国末期的天下之雄。但郑氏的执拗战胜了朝臣的规劝和敌人的威胁。终于在同年六月成行。

这次觐见是一场北明从藩镇时期到诸侯时期近三百年来都未有人见过的盛大巡游。虽然吴国主在燕、秦、齐等势力的胁迫下，最终只带了5000卫士和一些官员随行。但在这队伍中包罗了吴国海陆军事力量在那个时代的全部精锐，南洋的海兵、倭国的刀牌手、女真掷弹兵的早期营队，甚至还包括一个由“极东殷人”流亡贵族组成的，向中国皇帝伸冤借兵的队伍。并携带着吴人在这个地球上纵横百年来所获得无数珍宝，以及又用了近万名民夫运送的安南、高棉贡米。与之相对的，则是在藩镇节度使制度下被小规模械斗和转运使卡要下，四时常乱，在饥荒边缘长久徘徊的中原。

在郑昭的觐见使团归来后。他当即改其称号为”至尊“，吴国随即见证了一个南北流民向自己及殖民地不断涌入的快速发展时期。而在那之后，郑昭及其继承者也开始以更加严苛的力度推进集权主义的“专权变法”及土地商品化改革。并最终稳固了我们作为南朝尊主，总领万国的基业。吴人前进的脚步从未停下，直至今天......

pre_update_snapshot_occurrences.value: 朱班博战死，陈东阳遇刺，邓明舆投效，郑雕锦西奔。就连气吞万里的牧仲棠，也受限于北朝内忿，无暇南顾。金陵大殿上已无人能与郑吴至尊正面交锋。按照中国数千年以来的的历史，易姓革命只是早晚的事。但那些或是守旧或是革新的人们却总以为我们这个时代是超越了历史的。但梦想毕竟难以照进现实。\n\n当是时，恰逢吴主诞辰，南京百官不论出身，俱来杭州朝贺。以至于宁王系的明恭宗朝会上唯有故帅朱班博之子，兵部侍郎朱绛臣仍在。如此三日后，吴国辅郝廷疆与吴臣十人入金陵宫城。次日，明恭宗行效尧舜，禅让于吴。郑莒登基称帝，建号大吴。大赦，改元天演，史称天演帝、吴太宗。明恭宗朱阔彬降为明藩王，迁居福建崇明岛。旬月后，阔彬因会饮无度获罪。阔彬大惧，雇民船逃亡东洲。

相较于矛盾的全面爆发，富有决断力的南朝政治家们凭借一系列果断地决策延缓了帝国的瓦解。即使遭逢吴明易姓这样的大乱，各地督抚最终也决定不做出任何有效抵抗。接纳了吴国人对于明朝皇帝及其勋贵腐败透顶的说辞。从而维系了华南地区的脆弱和平。

虽然如此，这个从四百年的藩镇政治中爬出来的幸存者也失去了很多。战争与和平对峙的年代结束了。但反对者、藩国旧民之间的地域歧视、新的激进派政治团体仍在新时代的阴影下活动者。让这个国家向未来前进的道路蒙上了一层厚重的迷雾。
